title: Convolutional Neural Networks
description: Convolution, padding and stride, pooling, receptive fields and the main architectures from LeNet to ResNet.
overview: A fully connected layer treats an image as an unstructured list of numbers. A 224 × 224 color image has 150,528 values, and connecting them to even 1000 hidden units takes 150 million weights. Such a layer would also have to learn separately to detect an edge at every position in the image. Images have structure we can exploit: nearby pixels are related, and a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) build in these two properties. They are the standard architecture for images, video and audio, and the ideas (local connections, shared weights, hierarchy) carry over to many other domains.
objectives: Compute a 1D and 2D convolution (cross-correlation) by hand, and the output size for a given padding and stride.
Count the parameters of convolutional layers and compare them with fully connected layers.
Explain pooling and compute the receptive field of a stack of layers.
Describe the design of LeNet, VGG, ResNet and the role of 1×1 convolutions and skip connections.

sections.title: The convolution operation
body: A **convolutional layer** slides a small filter (kernel) over the input, and at each position computes the dot product between the filter and the patch beneath it. (What deep learning calls convolution is technically cross-correlation, since the filter is not flipped; since the filter is learned, the difference does not matter.)

body: For input I and a K × K filter W, the output is

Think of the filter as a small template for a pattern, held up to each part of the image in turn. Where the patch under it resembles the template the dot product is large, and where it does not the output is small or negative. The output is a map of where the pattern occurs.

example.title: A convolution step by step
example.problem: Slide the 2×2 filter with rows (1, 0) and (0, −1) over the 3×3 input with rows (1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 3), (2, 1, 1), with stride 1 and no padding.
solution: The output is 2×2, one value for each position of the filter. At each position, multiply the four filter entries by the four pixels beneath them and add.

The output is [[0, −1], [−1, 0]]. This filter compares each pixel with the one diagonally below and to its right, so its output is positive where the image gets darker along that diagonal and negative where it gets brighter.

example.title: A vertical edge detector
example.problem: A 6×6 image has pixel value 10 in its left three columns and 0 in its right three columns. Apply the filter with rows (1, 0, −1) three times (a vertical edge filter) with stride 1 and no padding.
solution: The output is 4×4. For a window covering columns j, j + 1, j + 2, the result is the sum of column j minus the sum of column j + 2, where each 3-row column sum is 30 for a column of 10s and 0 for 0s.

Every row of the output is (0, 30, 30, 0). The filter responds only where the image changes from bright to dark, so it detects the vertical edge. A CNN learns filters like this, and many others, from data.

body: A color image has 3 input **channels**. A filter spans all input channels: its size is K × K × C_in, and the dot product sums over all of them, producing one number per position. Using C_out different filters gives C_out output channels (a stack of **feature maps**), each detecting a different pattern. A layer has K·K·C_in·C_out weights plus C_out biases.

body.key: Two properties give CNNs their power. Local connectivity: each output depends only on a small patch. Weight sharing: the same filter is used at every position, so the number of parameters does not grow with the image size and a pattern is detected wherever it appears (translation equivariance: shifting the input shifts the output).

example.title: Convolutional versus fully connected parameters
example.problem: Compare the parameter counts of (a) a fully connected layer from a 224×224×3 image to 1000 units and (b) a 3×3 convolution from 64 channels to 128 channels.
example.solution: (a) 150,528 × 1000 + 1000 ≈ 150.5 million. (b) 3·3·64·128 + 128 = 73,728 + 128 = 73,856. The convolution has about 2000 times fewer parameters, for a layer that is applied at every position of an image.

sections.title: Padding, stride and output size
body: Without padding, each convolution shrinks the image by K − 1 pixels and ignores the border pixels. **Padding** adds a border of P zeros. **Stride** S moves the filter S pixels at a time, which downsamples the output. For an input of width W:

list: 'Valid' padding means P = 0. 'Same' padding uses P = (K − 1)/2 for odd K, so that with S = 1 the output has the same width as the input.
A stride of 2 halves the resolution, an alternative to pooling.
**Dilated** convolutions space the filter taps apart to see more context without extra parameters.

example.title: Output sizes
example.problem: Find the output width for (a) W = 32, K = 5, P = 2, S = 1 and (b) W = 224, K = 7, P = 3, S = 2.
example.solution: (a) (32 − 5 + 4)/1 + 1 = 32: the width is unchanged. (b) ⌊(224 − 7 + 6)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊223/2⌋ + 1 = 111 + 1 = 112. This is the first layer of the ResNet architecture, which halves 224 to 112.

sections.title: Pooling and receptive fields
body: A **pooling** layer summarizes each small window by one number and so shrinks the feature map. **Max pooling** keeps the largest value in each window. A 2×2 max pool with stride 2 halves the height and width. Pooling adds a little translation invariance (a small shift of the pattern leaves the pooled output unchanged), reduces the computation and enlarges the region each later unit can see. Pooling layers have no parameters. **Global average pooling** averages each whole feature map to a single number, turning the last feature maps into a vector for the classifier.

example.title: Max pooling
example.problem: Apply 2×2 max pooling with stride 2 to the 4×4 array with rows (1, 3, 2, 0), (4, 2, 1, 5), (0, 1, 3, 2), (2, 6, 4, 1).
example.solution: The four windows give max(1, 3, 4, 2) = 4, max(2, 0, 1, 5) = 5, max(0, 1, 2, 6) = 6 and max(3, 2, 4, 1) = 4. The output is [[4, 5], [6, 4]].

body: The **receptive field** of a unit is the region of the input that can influence it. A unit in the first 3×3 layer sees a 3×3 patch. After a second stacked 3×3 layer (stride 1) each unit sees 5×5, after a third, 7×7: in general 2n + 1 after n layers. Stride and pooling make the receptive field grow much faster in deeper layers.

This explains the VGG design principle: a stack of three 3×3 layers sees the same 7×7 region as one 7×7 layer, but with 3·(3·3)·C² = 27C² parameters instead of 49C², and it applies three nonlinearities instead of one.

body.key: Early layers detect local patterns (edges, colors), middle layers combine them into textures and parts, and late layers represent objects. The hierarchy emerges from stacking convolutions with growing receptive fields.

check.q: What is the receptive field of a unit after four stacked 3×3 convolutions with stride 1?

sections.title: Architectures: from LeNet to ResNet
body: A typical CNN alternates convolutions (with ReLU and often normalization) and downsampling, doubling the number of channels each time the resolution is halved, and ends with global pooling and a classifier.

body: A 1×1 convolution has no spatial extent. At each position it is a fully connected layer across the channels. It changes the number of channels cheaply and mixes information between channels. It is used to reduce channels before an expensive 3×3 convolution.

Simply stacking more layers made networks harder to train, and even worse on training error, long before overfitting could explain it. **ResNet** (He et al., 2015) adds a skip connection around each block of layers, so the block learns a correction to its input:

If the best thing for a block is to do nothing, F only has to learn zero. The derivative is I + ∂F/∂x, so gradients flow back along the identity path undiminished (see Vanishing and exploding gradients). ResNets with over 100 layers train easily, and skip connections now appear in nearly every deep architecture, including transformers. The bottleneck block of ResNet-50 uses a 1×1 convolution to reduce the channels, a 3×3 convolution, and a 1×1 convolution to restore them.

example.title: Why the bottleneck saves parameters
example.problem: A block works on 256 channels. Compare a plain 3×3 convolution 256 → 256 with a bottleneck: 1×1 (256 → 64), 3×3 (64 → 64), 1×1 (64 → 256). Ignore biases.
example.solution: Plain: 3·3·256·256 = 589,824. Bottleneck: 256·64 + 3·3·64·64 + 64·256 = 16,384 + 36,864 + 16,384 = 69,632. The bottleneck uses about 8.5 times fewer parameters.

check.a: gradients can flow through the identity path, so very deep networks train
wrong: it reduces the number of parameters
it removes the need for activations
it makes the network linear

sections.title: Training and using CNNs
body: Software turns a convolution into one large matrix multiplication (im2col: unroll every patch into a row, and the filters into columns), which GPUs execute very efficiently. Backpropagation through a convolution is another convolution: the gradient with respect to the input is a convolution of the upstream gradient with the flipped filter, and the gradient with respect to the filter is a convolution of the input with the upstream gradient. All the training techniques of the previous chapter apply, with batch normalization after each convolution.

Early layers learn general features (edges, textures) that are useful for almost any image task. **Transfer learning** exploits this. Take a network pretrained on a large data set such as ImageNet (1.2 million images, 1000 classes), replace the final layer with one for your classes, and then either train only the new layer (feature extraction) or train the whole network with a small learning rate (**fine-tuning**). With a few hundred labeled images this typically beats training from scratch by a wide margin.

list: **Object detection**: predict boxes and class labels for every object. Methods include region proposals (R-CNN family) and single-shot detectors (YOLO, SSD).

**Semantic segmentation**: classify every pixel. A fully convolutional network (a U-Net, for example) shrinks the image to gather context and then upsamples back, with skip connections that restore detail.
**Other data**: 1D convolutions apply to audio and time series, and 3D convolutions to video and volumes. Graph convolutions extend the idea to graphs.

**Vision transformers** divide an image into patches and process them with attention (see Attention and Transformers). With enough data they match or exceed CNNs, but CNNs remain efficient and strong when data are limited, because of the built-in inductive bias.

body.tip: Use data augmentation (random crops, flips, color changes) for image tasks. It adds the invariances that pooling only partly provides.

check.a: start from a pretrained network and fine-tune it
wrong: train a very deep network from scratch
use a fully connected network on the pixels

quiz.q: The filter with rows (1, −1) and (1, −1) is placed over the top-left 2×2 patch of an input whose rows begin (2, 0, …), (3, 1, …). What is that output value?
quiz.why: The dot product is 1·2 + (−1)·0 + 1·3 + (−1)·1 = 4. Forgetting the minus signs on the filter gives 6.

quiz.q: How many parameters (with biases) does a 3×3 convolution from 32 channels to 64 channels have?
quiz.why: Weights: 3·3·32·64 = 18,432, plus 64 biases gives 18,496. The count 2,112 is that of a 1×1 convolution.

quiz.q: The same 3×3 convolutional layer (32 input channels, 64 output channels) is applied to a 64×64 image and then to a 128×128 image. How does its parameter count change?
wrong: It becomes 4 times larger
It becomes 2 times larger
It depends on the stride and doubles with stride 1
quiz.why: The same filters are slid over every position, so the parameter count depends only on the kernel size and the channel counts, not on the image size.

quiz.q: An input of width 64 passes through a convolution with K = 3, P = 0 and S = 2. What is the output width?
quiz.why: ⌊(64 − 3 + 0)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊30.5⌋ + 1 = 31. Forgetting the floor gives 31.5, and forgetting the + 1 gives 30.

quiz.q: A 7×7 convolution with stride 1 must keep the width of its input unchanged. How much zero padding P on each side is needed?
quiz.why: 'Same' padding uses P = (K − 1)/2 = 3, so that W_out = W − 7 + 6 + 1 = W.

quiz.q: The 4×4 array with rows (7, 2, 1, 3), (0, 5, 4, 4), (6, 1, 2, 0), (3, 2, 8, 1) goes through 2×2 max pooling with stride 2. The output is
quiz.why: Each non-overlapping 2×2 window keeps its largest value. The first wrong option is average pooling and the second is min pooling.

quiz.q: Which statement about a shift of the input image by 2 pixels is correct for a convolutional layer with stride 1?
quiz.a: The output feature map shifts by 2 pixels as well
wrong: The output stays exactly the same
The output is reflected about the vertical axis
The output changes in a way that cannot be predicted from the shift
quiz.why: Weight sharing makes a convolution translation equivariant. Invariance, an unchanged output, is only partly added by pooling.

quiz.q: Two 3×3 convolutions (stride 1) are followed by a 3×3 convolution with stride 2 and another 3×3 convolution. What is the receptive field of a unit in the last layer?
quiz.why: The first two layers give 5. The stride-2 layer adds 2 to give 7 and doubles the step size, so the last layer adds 2 × 2 = 4, giving 11.

quiz.q: Two stacked 3×3 convolutions with C channels in and out see the same region as one 5×5 convolution. How do their parameter counts compare (ignoring biases)?
wrong: 9C² against 25C²
25C² against 18C²
36C² against 25C²
quiz.why: Two 3×3 layers have 2·9·C² = 18C² weights and a 5×5 layer has 25C². The stack also applies two nonlinearities instead of one.

quiz.q: How many parameters (with biases) does a 1×1 convolution from 256 channels to 64 channels have, on a feature map of any size?
quiz.why: A 1×1 convolution is a fully connected layer across channels: 256·64 weights plus 64 biases. The number does not depend on the spatial size of the map.

quiz.q: A bottleneck block works on 128 channels: a 1×1 convolution (128 → 32), a 3×3 convolution (32 → 32), and a 1×1 convolution (32 → 128). Ignoring biases, how many parameters does it have?
quiz.why: 4,096 + 9,216 + 4,096 = 17,408. A plain 3×3 convolution from 128 to 128 would need 147,456, and 13,312 leaves out the final restoring 1×1 layer.

quiz.q: In a residual block y = x + F(x), what must F compute if the best thing for the block is to do nothing?
wrong: The identity function F(x) = x
The negative of the input, F(x) = −x
A constant equal to the mean of the input
quiz.why: The skip connection already supplies x, so F only has to output 0. A plain block would have to learn the identity map, which is harder.

quiz.q: A plain 56-layer network has higher training error than a 20-layer one. Why does this point to an optimization problem and not to overfitting?
quiz.a: Overfitting would show as low training error, and this network cannot even fit its training data as well
wrong: Overfitting always makes the training error higher
The deeper network has fewer parameters, so it must underfit by capacity
The test error is always lower for deeper networks
quiz.why: Overfitting lowers training error while raising validation error. Higher training error for a larger model means it is harder to train, which residual connections fix.

quiz.q: The gradient of the loss with respect to a convolutional filter is computed as
quiz.a: a convolution of the layer's input with the upstream gradient
wrong: a convolution of the flipped filter with the upstream gradient
the sum of all input pixels times the upstream gradient
the elementwise product of the filter and the input
quiz.why: Backpropagation through a convolution is another convolution. The flipped-filter form gives the gradient with respect to the input instead.

quiz.q: What is the difference between feature extraction and fine-tuning in transfer learning?
quiz.a: Feature extraction trains only the new final layer, while fine-tuning also updates the pretrained layers at a small learning rate
wrong: Feature extraction trains all layers from random weights, while fine-tuning freezes everything
Feature extraction uses the test set, while fine-tuning uses the training set
Fine-tuning replaces the pretrained network with a smaller one
quiz.why: Both start from a network pretrained on a large data set and replace the last layer. They differ in how much of the pretrained network is allowed to change.

quiz.q: Why does a U-Net add skip connections from the shrinking path to the upsampling path?
quiz.a: To restore fine spatial detail lost when the image was downsampled
wrong: To reduce the number of parameters in the classifier
To let boxes and class labels be predicted for each object
To avoid vanishing gradients in the final fully connected layer
quiz.why: Semantic segmentation needs a label for every pixel. The downsampling path gathers context but loses location detail, which the skip connections bring back.

quiz.q: With only a small amount of training data, why might a CNN beat a vision transformer?
quiz.a: Locality and weight sharing are built in, so less data is needed to learn them
wrong: A CNN has far more parameters, so it fits small data better
A transformer cannot process images divided into patches
A CNN does not need any training data
quiz.why: The inductive bias of a CNN matches image structure. A vision transformer must learn such structure from data and matches or beats CNNs only with enough of it.

summary: A convolutional layer slides a small learned filter over the input. Local connectivity and weight sharing cut the parameters drastically and give translation equivariance. A layer has K·K·C_in·C_out weights.
The output width is ⌊(W − K + 2P)/S⌋ + 1. Padding preserves the size, and stride downsamples.
Pooling summarizes windows (max or average) and adds a little invariance. The receptive field grows with depth: 2n + 1 for n stacked 3×3 layers.
1×1 convolutions mix channels cheaply. ResNet's skip connection y = x + F(x) lets gradients bypass layers, enabling networks of hundreds of layers.
Transfer learning from a pretrained network is the default for small data sets. CNN ideas extend to detection, segmentation, audio and video.

problems.q: A 32×32×3 image goes through conv(5×5, 6 filters, no padding, stride 1), then 2×2 max pooling (stride 2). Give the output shape and the parameter count of the convolution.
problems.solution: Conv output: 32 − 5 + 1 = 28, so 28×28×6. Pooling halves it to 14×14×6. Parameters: 5·5·3·6 + 6 = 456.

problems.q: Convolve the 1D signal (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) with the filter (1, 0, −1) (stride 1, no padding).
A network stacks three 3×3 convolutions (stride 1) and then a 2×2 max pool (stride 2), then two more 3×3 convolutions. What is the receptive field in the input pixels of a unit in the last layer?
problems.solution: After three 3×3 convs: 7. The pool adds (2 − 1) × 1 = 1, giving 8, and doubles the stride to 2. Each of the next two 3×3 layers adds (3 − 1) × 2 = 4, giving 8 + 4 + 4 = 16.

problems.q: Output width for W = 100, K = 3, P = 1, S = 2.
A skip connection y = x + F(x) has F with Jacobian J. If the loss gradient at y is g, what is the gradient at x?
problems.solution: ∂L/∂x = (I + J)ᵀg = g + Jᵀg. The term g passes straight through, whatever F does.
